caption: A composite grid of twenty panels from Josef Albers' 'Homage to the Square' series. Each panel features a standardized geometric composition of three or four nested squares. The series explores the 'interaction of color,' demonstrating how the perception of a single hue changes based on its proximity to others. Albers used these consistent forms to investigate optical effects like simultaneous contrast and spatial depth, where colors may appear to recede or advance. The grid showcases a wide spectrum of color relationships, from monochromatic harmonies to vibrant, clashing contrasts.

caption: An 18th-century Polish devotional engraving serving as a frontispiece or illustration for a religious text titled 'DRELOWANIE CZWARTE' concerning the Blessed Sacrament of the Altar. Flanking the altar are an angel with a trumpet on the left and a female personification, likely Faith or Charity, on the right holding a plate of bread. caption:
This is Saint Veronica with the Sudarium, painted around 1500 by the Master of the Legend of Saint Ursula — an as yet unidentified late 15th-century Flemish master who was one of the most important masters working in Bruges in the late 15th century and a contemporary of Hans Memling. 
Veronica, with her exotic headgear and flapping headscarves, has veiled her eyes and looks down at the cloth she holds. It is said to portray the true face of Christ — the Vera Icon — which is in fact the origin of Veronica's name.
The panel has an arched top, with the saint set against a gilt background. Her elaborate clothing and headdress are bejeweled, and the veils on either side of her head are animated as if in the wind. Christ is shown looking straight ahead at the viewer, depicted in exacting detail. 
The elongated bodies and egg-shaped heads are typical of the Ursula Master's style, clearly visible here.

caption:
A ceiling fresco depicting an allegory of Astrology, featuring a central female figure in flowing yellow and white drapery, surrounded by several putti. One putto holds an armillary sphere, while others interact with books and scrolls, specifically one scroll with the word 'ASTROLOGIA'. The scene is set against a backdrop of blue sky and white clouds, enclosed within dark architectural framing.

Compare claude.ai with the prompt addition "Escorial"
This is the Astrologia (Astrology) fresco from the Royal Library of El Escorial. The library ceiling fresco cycle was painted by the Milanese artist Pellegrino Tibaldi (1527–1596), based on a humanist program devised by the library's first librarian. The vault is divided into seven zones representing the seven liberal arts — the Trivium (Grammar, Rhetoric, and Dialectic) and the Quadrivium (Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, and Astrology). Each discipline is personified by an allegorical figure. caption:
Castello della Manta: Fountain of Youth

Authorship & Date
The work is attributed to the anonymous "Master of Castello della Manta" and was completed soon after 1420. It was commissioned by Valerano of Saluzzo, the illegitimate son of the Marchese Tommaso III, between 1411 and 1416. 

Subject & Iconography
On the southern wall of the Sala Baronale, the myth of eternal youth is depicted by the fountain of youth, surmounted by the god of Love. 
The central Gothic fountain dominates the composition, topped by a small figure of Cupid (the god of Love). Around it, a lively crowd of figures in rich Late Gothic dress approaches from both sides — nobles, monks, elderly men and women — all eager to bathe and be restored to youth.
In the fresco, travelers are shedding their clothes and stripping off their stockings. On the side, some figures are climbing into the water. Inside the basin, rejuvenated couples are engaged in playful interactions. 

The lush green trees, the richly colored garments (reds, blues, yellows, whites), and the animated crowd give the scene a festive, almost theatrical energy — a rare and vivid window into 15th-century courtly imagination.

caption:
This is a richly illuminated manuscript page depicting Christ as Salvator Mundi ("Savior of the World"), a common iconographic type in late medieval and Renaissance art, likely from a Book of Hours or similar devotional manuscript.
Central image:
Christ is shown half-length, facing forward, with long brown hair and a forked beard
He wears a rose/pink robe (possibly a chemise or tunic) with a bejeweled clasp at the neck featuring a large cross-shaped brooch with colored gemstones
His right hand is raised in a gesture of benediction (blessing), with two fingers extended
His left hand holds a globe/orb (representing the world) topped with a cross — the defining attribute of the Salvator Mundi type
A radiant gold halo with cruciform rays surrounds his head, set against a deep blue background
The blue field is filled with fine gold radiating lines suggesting divine light or glory

Lower register:
A smaller framed scene beneath shows a narrative episode, appears to depict a Way to Calvary / Road to Golgotha scene — figures with ladders, tools, and a group of soldiers or workers, possibly preparing the cross or engaged in the Passion narrative

Left border:
An ornate architectural frame in gold with grotesque/candelabra-style ornament (scrollwork, vase-like elements)
Two small grisaille (monochrome) figures stand in niches within the border, likely representing prophets or saints, rendered in a statue-like grayscale technique typical of Flemish/Netherlandish manuscript illumination
